attribution.note: Marcus directly asserts both products' nonarrival.

semantics.note: Faithful when anchored to the October 20 publication date and ordinary customer availability.

contract.note: Customer availability is an ordinary reading of arrival in this product-shipment discussion. Distinguishing previews from releases is fair.

Company disclosure of December customer availability; it does not explicitly document the target day's status.
Company disclosure of an August 2025 launch. The contract excludes treating this later event as October 2024 outcome evidence.

reviews.rationale: The chronology is consistent with Marcus's statement, but the packet lacks a record establishing both products' availability on October 20 under the contract's explicit date rule. No qualifying contradiction is supplied.

attribution.note: Marcus states both the expense and capability assessments in his own voice.

semantics.note: The normalization preserves the two factual assessments. Omitting his subjective interest in the model does not alter them.

contract.note: Serving expense and broad reliability are reasonable plain readings in context. Targeting the available preview is fair; neither component has an explicit numerical threshold.

evidence.note: Company disclosure supports contemporary limitations on common uses. It does not establish operating expense or quantify distance from a general solution.
Company preference evaluations support uneven suitability across tasks, while also reporting reasoning strengths. Preference is not a general reliability measure.
Qualitative expense language and customer pricing do not establish matched provider operating costs.
Independent evaluation cautions that many failures may reflect agent setup. It neither establishes broad reliability nor refutes limitations of the released system.

reviews.rationale: The packet supports limitations but does not establish their asserted breadth or matched operating expense. Reasoning strengths and METR's setup caveat limit stronger conclusions. Neither the conjunction nor its contradiction is established.

attribution.note: Marcus endorses these observations and the qualified analogy, although he attributes others' stronger Theranos comparison to them.

semantics.note: The normalization preserves unmet expectations, customer access, and the qualified rhetorical conclusion. It does not assert universal disappointment.

contract.note: The contract reasonably tests shipment and substantial unmet expectations while treating the analogy as rhetoric. It preserves the distinction between some disappointed expectations and universal dissatisfaction.

evidence.note: Company disclosure establishes customer access to GPT-4o within the historical period. It does not establish the expectations component.
Company disclosure of public beta access supports continued product shipment and customer trials, without establishing fulfillment of all advertised capabilities.
The attributed company statement documents a specific delay. It does not establish the scope or substantial degree of unmet expectations asserted.

reviews.rationale: Customer-access disclosures support the shipment component. One documented delay does not settle the substantial expectations shortfall, and the analogy has no separate factual test. The full claim remains unresolved; no component is established as false.
